patch.objective: Apply the duty to warn or protect when a client threatens an identifiable person

sources.cite: Washington DOH, Jurisprudence Exam RCW and WAC References (psychologists): the laws the Washington psychology jurisprudence exam draws on; WAC 246-924-230 requires passing it within the first continuing education cycle after initial licensure
sources.note: Read 2026-11-14 for the course (REQ-287). DOH publishes no outline, format or passing score; RCW 71.05.120(3) is not on DOH's list and is used because the duty-to-protect objective needs the Washington rule.

sources.cite: Chapter 70.02 RCW: 70.02.050(1)(c) a provider may disclose without authorization to a person able to prevent or lessen a serious and imminent threat, including the target; 70.02.230 mental health records stay confidential except as the chapter allows, such as to law enforcement and a person whose health and safety the patient has threatened (70.02.230 changes on 2027-06-30)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-14 for the course (REQ-287); the wording is the course's record of the sections, not a quotation.

sources.cite: APA, Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct (2002, amended 2010 and 2016, effective 2017): 4.01, 4.02, 4.04, 4.05, 10.01
sources.note: The current code. APA's Ethics Code Task Force has a revised draft under comment review (expected late 2026 or early 2027) and nothing new has been adopted (apa.org/ethics/task-force, updated July 2026).

sources.cite: RCW 71.05.120(3) (amended 2019 c 446 s 22 and 2020 c 302 s 11): no relief from 'the duty to warn or to take reasonable precautions to provide protection from violent behavior where the patient has communicated an actual threat of physical violence against a reasonably identifiable victim or victims'; the duty 'is discharged if reasonable efforts are made to communicate the threat to the victim or victims and to law enforcement personnel'
sources.note: Read on the Legislature's site; the duty-to-warn sentence is now subsection (3) (it was (2) before the 2016-2020 amendments).

sources.cite: Volk v. DeMeerleer, Washington Supreme Court No. 91387-1 (en banc, 2016): an outpatient relationship can be a special relationship (Restatement (Second) of Torts s 315); under Petersen v. State, 100 Wn.2d 421 (1983), the professional must use reasonable care, consistent with the standards of the profession, to protect the patient's foreseeable victims; foreseeability is a question of fact
sources.note: The University of Washington's 2025 duty-to-protect teaching slides (Piel, 15 Aug 2025) still present Volk as the outpatient standard and report that RCW 71.05.120(3) was held not to apply outside involuntary commitment; that point is the slides'. The slip opinion was read 2026-11-16 (courts.wa.gov PDF, summarizing fetch with quotes): the majority rests the outpatient duty on Restatement s 315 ('a duty of reasonable care to act consistent with the standards of the mental health profession and to protect the foreseeable victims'), holds foreseeability a question of fact, and mentions RCW 71.05.120 only in describing the defendants' argument; it does not itself rule on the statute's reach. SB 5800 (2017), which would have narrowed the duty to an actual threat against an identifiable person, died in committee (LegiScan). Reporter citation not confirmed on the page read.

sources.cite: Piel J. Legal duty to protect. UW Behavioral Health Institute TeleBH series, 15 Aug 2025

UW School of Law, Volk v. DeMeerleer study for the Washington House Judiciary Committee, 1 Dec 2017: Volk 'substantially changed the duty to protect and the duty to warn in Washington in the outpatient context'

Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California, 17 Cal.3d 425 (1976): a duty to use reasonable care to protect the intended victim, which may be discharged by warning the victim, notifying police or other reasonable steps; 'The protective privilege ends where the public peril begins' (17 Cal.3d at 442)

HHS, HIPAA FAQ 520 and 45 CFR 164.512(j): disclosure without authorization when necessary to prevent or lessen a serious and imminent threat, to a person reasonably able to prevent or lessen it (including the target and law enforcement), consistent with applicable law and ethics
